That first one—can’t miss it, the cruise ship, gliding in like it owns the whole bay. White hull flashing in the sun, passengers peering out like they’re on vacation even before they’ve tied up. It’s always a rush with those. Gotta keep the gangways straight, make sure the lines are secure, and watch out for the sheer size of her hull. One slip and it could knock half the smaller boats aside. I’m thinking logistics—where’s customs ready? Did maintenance finish inspecting the berthing lines? People get antsy when they’ve paid for a cruise and are just itching to disembark. Gotta stay calm and be thorough.

Behind her, that red-accented ferry. Less glitz, but plenty of pressure. That’s a tight window for turn-around—folks on board are probably just looking to get to their homes or jobs. Need to check the loading ramp’s functioning, verify passenger headcounts, make sure the cars aren’t too heavy on one side. And always, always listen for any last-minute calls from the bridge; captains like to be clear on docking instructions. It’s a bit like a well-oiled machine, but a jammed gear somewhere means delayed commutes for a hundred people.

Then there’s the trawler, bobbing at the back, paint faded by salt and sun. This one’s more familiar territory. The skipper usually waves as he lines up, wants clear rails and a quick check that the winch is operational. Less urgency, but still can’t rush—fishermen hate being kept waiting when they’ve hauled in a heavy catch. Need to make sure the ice holds are stocked and that the crew’s gear isn’t in the way. Sometimes I chat with them; they’ve got stories you won’t hear on the big ships.

All three, different rhythms. Big ships bring spectacle, ferries bring schedules, trawlers bring stories. My job’s just the same, but the details never quite repeat. The trawler was a sinister and ancient craft, with broken bulwarks and a rust-red hull, and it steered so close to the pier that I could have thrown a rope on board from where I stood. I looked for some sign of the master or mate, but the deck was empty. There were only two figures, one at the bow and one at the stern,-both crouched down as though they were searching for something in the water. I watched them narrowly, but I could not be sure whether they were men or some new kind of mannequin. Some quitemodation had been made amidships, for there was a sort of imperfect awning stretched across the deck, but this hid any detail of the trawler's cargo from my view.
As the vessel passed the end of the pier its speed slackened, so that for a moment the three boats—-the dredger with its drifting pall of silt, the white police launch, and the sinister red trawler with its invisible cargo-were abreast of one another. Then the trawler gave a sudden lurch and gathered way again, so that it was soon nearly a quarter of a mile ahead of the others. I watched it as it angled across the harbor entrance and saw the dull flush on its obscured deck change to a livid grey. Then itchecks for a moment in midstream while the man at the stern bends to tweak the propeller, and during that interval I lost sight of it behind a small rocky outcrop.
I waited for a while, wondering if it would reappear further along the coast or perhaps put back into the harbor, but no hull or funnel broke the distant horizon. Then I turned back to the waterfront.

Cycling a battery means charging it and then discharging it, charge being the total amount of electricity stored in or delivered by the cell in Ampere-hours (usually represented by the symbol Q). To get an extract PV plot you periodically measure the cell voltage (V) as a function of charge moved into or out of the cell, normally as a function of charge per unit mass of cell (i.e. specific charge - normally written as q, lower case). Specific charge is just the total charge divided by the mass of 'active material' in the cell. Active material is generally the part of the cell where the Li+ ions move from one electrode to the other when charging or discharging. You will often see specific capacity and specific charge used interchangeably - the relationship between charge and capacity is a constant of proportionality defined by the time over which the charge was applied (i.e. how long the battery was charged or discharged at a given current). 

Extract PV plots are very useful for comparing different cells to one another, for example so that you can identify the voltage at which 'useful' Li+ ions can no longer be inserted into (or extracted from) the cell. 512.prompt: I opened the window and heard a distant bell. Beneath it, I could also hear
512.completion:
the pitter-patter of tiny raindrops.  I took a deep breath.

Early mornings like these always give me mixed feelings. In one hand, I feel bad for what I have to do. On the other hand, the cool air and the smell of the wet soil are exhilarating. At moments like these, all my problems and worries go away.

Well, most of them, that is. There was not-so-minor problem I had to deal with today. Another noise joined the rain and bell sounds — the rumbling and screeching of heavy vehicles. I took another deep breath and focused all my attention on staying steady. I forced my hands to stop shaking.  There was no way I would let my fears take control over me.

Nonetheless, I could feel a few tears rolling down my cheeks. I wished I had never heard that sound again, but I realized that wasn't exactly true. I just wished I had never agreed to do what I was about to do now.

Perhaps "agreed" is not the proper word. I didn’t really have a choice in the matter. I had learned early on that resisting would only bring more trouble. Still, it was very different to accept something when you know you don't have any options, as opposed to when you know doing something will bring you pleasure. And I had learned in even earlier that those two feelings often go hand in hand.

Soon all of my relatives would wake up and start getting ready for the day. Some of them would make their way to the kitchen. A few of them would pour themselves a cup of warm tea. I could already imagine the mixed aromas of fresh bread and steeping leaves.

However, I knew that the moment someone among them stepped outside, they would hear the same noises I was hearing. And when that happened, things would start becoming chaotic. I could already picture aunt Martha running around looking for her hairband. Uncle Bret would probably be blaming the government again.

Calm down, I told myself. You've been through this before. Just go through the motions and before you know it will all be over. I took one last deep breath before leaving the house. This was it. I was ready. Or at least, as ready as I would ever be.
